content: The pharmacokinetics of progesterone in postmenopausal women are generally consistent with those observed in this population. Distribution: Progesterone is approximately 96% to 99% bound to serum proteins, primarily to serum albumin (50% to 54%) and transcortin (43% to 48%). Metabolism: Progesterone undergoes primary metabolism in the liver, where it is largely converted to pregnanediols and pregnanolones. These metabolites are conjugated in the liver to glucuronide and sulfate derivatives. Progesterone metabolites excreted in the bile may undergo deconjugation and further metabolism in the intestine through reduction, dehydroxylation, and epimerization. Excretion: The glucuronide and sulfate conjugates of pregnanediol and pregnanolone are excreted in the bile and urine. Progesterone metabolites are primarily eliminated by the kidneys. Those excreted in the bile may undergo enterohepatic recycling or be excreted in the feces. Special Populations: The pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM Capsules have not been evaluated in patients with low body weight or obesity. Hepatic Insufficiency: The effect of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM Capsules has not been studied. Renal Insufficiency: The effect of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM Capsules has not been studied. Food-Drug Interaction: Concomitant ingestion of food increases the bioavailability of PROMETRIUM Capsules compared to administration in a fasting state, as observed in postmenopausal women receiving a 200 mg dose. Ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, may increase the bioavailability of progesterone. However, the clinical relevance of these in vitro findings remains unknown. Nonclinical Toxicology: Carcinogenesis: Progesterone has not been tested for carcinogenicity via oral administration in animals. When implanted in female mice, progesterone induced mammary carcinomas, ovarian granulosa cell tumors, and endometrial stromal sarcomas. In dogs, long-term intramuscular injections caused nodular hyperplasia and both benign and malignant mammary tumors. Subcutaneous or intramuscular injections of progesterone reduced latency periods and increased the incidence of mammary tumors in rats previously treated with a chemical carcinogen. Mutagenesis: Progesterone did not demonstrate evidence of genotoxicity in in vitro studies for point mutations or chromosomal damage. However, in vivo studies in mice showed positive results for chromosomal damage at oral doses of 1000 mg/kg and 2000 mg/kg. Impairment of Fertility: Exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in various species. High doses administered over extended periods are expected to impair fertility until treatment cessation. Clinical Studies on Endometrial Effects: In a randomized, double-blind clinical trial, 358 postmenopausal women with intact uteri received treatment for up to 36 months. The treatment groups included PROMETRIUM Capsules plus conjugated estrogens (n=120), conjugated estrogens alone (n=119), or placebo (n=119). The majority of participants in all groups were Caucasian (87% or more). The incidence of endometrial hyperplasia over three years of treatment was significantly lower in the PROMETRIUM Capsules plus conjugated estrogens group (6%) compared to the conjugated estrogens-only group (64%). The time to diagnosis of endometrial hyperplasia over 36 months was graphically illustrated, showing a significantly higher proportion of hyperplasia in the conjugated estrogens-only group compared to the combination treatment group. Discontinuation rates due to hyperplasia over the 36-month treatment period were also reported, further supporting the protective effect of PROMETRIUM Capsules when combined with conjugated estrogens.
